findings.finding: Week-over-week booked gross revenue is highly volatile, but the largest surge in the sample occurs in 2015-03-16: gross revenue reaches 37,703.66 and gross profit is positive at 33,564.06, indicating that major revenue spikes are accompanied by gross profit growth.
findings.question: How is booked gross revenue trending week over week (and is it accompanied by gross profit growth)?
findings.sql: WITH weekly AS (SELECT DATE_TRUNC('WEEK', order_date) AS week_start, SUM(sales) AS booked_gross_revenue, SUM(profit) AS booked_gross_profit FROM orders GROUP BY 1) SELECT week_start, booked_gross_revenue, booked_gross_profit, (booked_gross_revenue - LAG(booked_gross_revenue) OVER (ORDER BY week_start)) AS revenue_wow_change, (booked_gross_profit - LAG(booked_gross_profit) OVER (ORDER BY week_start)) AS profit_wow_change FROM weekly ORDER BY week_start

findings.finding: AOV and units per order moved up together: from 2015-03-02 to 2015-03-16, AOV surged from 321.95 to 2,217.86 (+1,895.91) while units per order rose from 7.46 to 12.41 (+4.95), indicating customers bought higher-value items alongside buying more units per order.
findings.question: Are customers buying fewer/higher-value items—i.e., how do AOV and units per order move together over time?
findings.sql: WITH weekly AS (SELECT DATE_TRUNC('WEEK', order_date) AS week_start, SUM(sales) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT order_id), 0) AS aov, SUM(quantity) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT order_id), 0) AS units_per_order FROM orders GROUP BY 1) SELECT week_start, aov, units_per_order, (aov - LAG(aov) OVER (ORDER BY week_start)) AS aov_wow_change, (units_per_order - LAG(units_per_order) OVER (ORDER BY week_start)) AS units_per_order_wow_change FROM weekly ORDER BY week_start

findings.finding: From the visible weeks, gross profit margin is improving (14 of 20 weeks show positive gross profit margin change), but it only aligns with the sign of average discount-rate change about 9 of 19 weeks (~47%), indicating weak alignment.
findings.question: Is gross profit margin improving or deteriorating, and how much of that aligns with average discount rate changes?
findings.sql: WITH weekly AS (SELECT DATE_TRUNC('WEEK', order_date) AS week_start, SUM(profit) / NULLIF(SUM(sales), 0) AS gross_margin_pct, AVG(discount) AS avg_discount_rate FROM orders GROUP BY 1) SELECT week_start, gross_margin_pct, avg_discount_rate, (gross_margin_pct - LAG(gross_margin_pct) OVER (ORDER BY week_start)) AS gross_margin_wow_change, (avg_discount_rate - LAG(avg_discount_rate) OVER (ORDER BY week_start)) AS discount_wow_change FROM weekly ORDER BY week_start

findings.finding: Technology → Phones generates the most revenue ($330,007.05) with positive profit ($44,515.73) and a relatively high return of 0.087224.
findings.question: Which categories and sub-categories generate the most revenue and profit, and are they also associated with higher returns?
findings.sql: WITH cat_profit AS (SELECT category, sub_category, SUM(sales) AS revenue, SUM(profit) AS profit FROM orders GROUP BY 1, 2), cat_returns AS (SELECT o.category, o.sub_category, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS eligible_orders, COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN r.returned THEN o.order_id END) AS returned_orders, COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN r.returned THEN o.order_id END) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id), 0) AS return_rate FROM orders AS o LEFT JOIN returns AS r ON o.order_id = r.order_id GROUP BY 1, 2) SELECT cp.category, cp.sub_category, cp.revenue, cp.profit, cr.return_rate FROM cat_profit AS cp JOIN cat_returns AS cr ON cp.category = cr.category AND cp.sub_category = cr.sub_category ORDER BY cp.revenue DESC

findings.finding: Same Day shipping has the highest return rate at 0.07197 (~7.2%), exceeding First Class (0.068615 ~6.9%) and other modes like Second Class (0.057054) and Standard Class (0.056112), suggesting expectation/fulfillment issues are most pronounced for Same Day.
findings.question: Do any shipping modes show systematically higher return rates (suggesting expectation/fulfillment issues)?
findings.sql: WITH ship_returns AS (SELECT o.ship_mode, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS eligible_orders, COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN r.returned THEN o.order_id END) AS returned_orders, COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN r.returned THEN o.order_id END) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id), 0) AS return_rate FROM orders AS o LEFT JOIN returns AS r ON o.order_id = r.order_id GROUP BY 1) SELECT ship_mode, return_rate, returned_orders, eligible_orders FROM ship_returns ORDER BY return_rate DESC, eligible_orders DESC

findings.finding: Home Office has the highest profit margin (0.140343) while also showing a relatively low return rate (0.053905), making it the best profitability profile among the segments with acceptable returns.
findings.question: Which customer segment (Consumer / Corporate / Home Office) has the best profitability profile (profit margin) while maintaining an acceptable return rate?
findings.sql: WITH seg_profit AS (SELECT segment, SUM(profit) / NULLIF(SUM(sales), 0) AS profit_margin_pct FROM orders GROUP BY 1), seg_returns AS (SELECT o.segment, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS eligible_orders, COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN r.returned THEN o.order_id END) AS returned_orders, COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN r.returned THEN o.order_id END) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id), 0) AS return_rate FROM orders AS o LEFT JOIN returns AS r ON o.order_id = r.order_id GROUP BY 1) SELECT sp.segment, sp.profit_margin_pct, sr.return_rate, sr.returned_orders, sr.eligible_orders FROM seg_profit AS sp JOIN seg_returns AS sr ON sp.segment = sr.segment ORDER BY sp.profit_margin_pct DESC, sr.return_rate ASC

findings.sql: WITH phones_sales_by_ship_mode AS (SELECT o.ship_mode, SUM(o.sales) AS phones_sales FROM orders AS o WHERE o.category = 'Technology' AND o.sub_category = 'Phones' GROUP BY 1), phones_total_sales AS (SELECT SUM(o.sales) AS phones_total_sales FROM orders AS o WHERE o.category = 'Technology' AND o.sub_category = 'Phones'), phones_return_rate_by_ship_mode AS (SELECT o.ship_mode, COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN r.returned THEN o.order_id END) * 100.0 / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id), 0) AS phones_return_rate_pct FROM orders AS o LEFT JOIN returns AS r ON o.order_id = r.order_id WHERE o.category = 'Technology' AND o.sub_category = 'Phones' GROUP BY 1) SELECT p0.phones_total_sales, sbsm.ship_mode, sbsm.phones_sales, sbsm.phones_sales / NULLIF(p0.phones_total_sales, 0) * 100.0 AS pct_of_phones_total_sales, rr.phones_return_rate_pct FROM phones_total_sales AS p0 JOIN phones_sales_by_ship_mode AS sbsm ON TRUE LEFT JOIN phones_return_rate_by_ship_mode AS rr ON rr.ship_mode = sbsm.ship_mode WHERE sbsm.ship_mode = 'First Class' OR sbsm.ship_mode IN ('Second Class', 'Standard Class', 'Same Day') ORDER BY CASE sbsm.ship_mode WHEN 'First Class' THEN 1 WHEN 'Second Class' THEN 2 WHEN 'Standard Class' THEN 3 WHEN 'Same Day' THEN 4 ELSE 5 END

findings.finding: Across the combined view, Same Day is high at 0.07197 in one context but low at 0.055556 in another (while the highest rate observed is 0.072917 for First Class), showing a reversal/shift in which shipping modes are most return-prone depending on the time-context being compared.

findings.sql: WITH max_dates AS (SELECT MAX(order_date) AS max_order_date FROM orders), rate_overall AS (SELECT o.ship_mode, CAST(COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN r.returned THEN o.order_id END) AS DOUBLE) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id), 0) AS return_rate_overall FROM orders AS o LEFT JOIN returns AS r ON o.order_id = r.order_id WHERE o.ship_mode IN ('Same Day', 'First Class') GROUP BY o.ship_mode), rate_last_12_months AS (SELECT o.ship_mode, CAST(COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN r.returned THEN o.order_id END) AS DOUBLE) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id), 0) AS return_rate_last_12_months FROM orders AS o LEFT JOIN returns AS r ON o.order_id = r.order_id CROSS JOIN max_dates AS md WHERE o.ship_mode IN ('Same Day', 'First Class') AND o.order_date >= md.max_order_date - INTERVAL '365' DAY GROUP BY o.ship_mode) SELECT COALESCE(oo.return_rate_overall, 0) AS same_day_return_rate_overall, COALESCE(fl.return_rate_last_12_months, 0) AS first_class_return_rate_last_12_months, COALESCE(of.return_rate_overall, 0) AS first_class_return_rate_overall, COALESCE(sl.return_rate_last_12_months, 0) AS same_day_return_rate_last_12_months, (COALESCE(oo.return_rate_overall, 0) > COALESCE(of.return_rate_overall, 0)) AS same_day_higher_overall_than_first_class, (COALESCE(fl.return_rate_last_12_months, 0) > COALESCE(sl.return_rate_last_12_months, 0)) AS first_class_higher_in_last_12_months_than_same_day FROM (SELECT * FROM rate_overall WHERE ship_mode = 'Same Day') AS oo CROSS JOIN (SELECT * FROM rate_last_12_months WHERE ship_mode = 'First Class') AS fl CROSS JOIN (SELECT * FROM rate_overall WHERE ship_mode = 'First Class') AS of CROSS JOIN (SELECT * FROM rate_last_12_months WHERE ship_mode = 'Same Day') AS sl

findings.sql: WITH weekly_margin AS (SELECT DATE_TRUNC('WEEK', o.order_date) AS week_start, SUM(o.profit) AS total_profit, SUM(o.sales) AS total_sales, SUM(o.profit) / NULLIF(SUM(o.sales), 0) AS gross_profit_margin FROM orders AS o GROUP BY 1), weekly_margin_with_change AS (SELECT wm.week_start, wm.gross_profit_margin, wm.gross_profit_margin - LAG(wm.gross_profit_margin) OVER (ORDER BY wm.week_start) AS gross_profit_margin_change FROM weekly_margin AS wm), positive_margin_weeks AS (SELECT week_start FROM weekly_margin_with_change WHERE gross_profit_margin_change > 0), returned_orders_by_week AS (SELECT DATE_TRUNC('WEEK', o.order_date) AS week_start, COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN r.returned THEN o.order_id END) AS returned_orders_total, COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN r.returned AND o.ship_mode = 'Same Day' THEN o.order_id END) AS returned_orders_same_day FROM orders AS o LEFT JOIN returns AS r ON o.order_id = r.order_id WHERE NOT o.order_date IS NULL GROUP BY 1) SELECT rw.week_start, CAST(rw.returned_orders_same_day AS DOUBLE) / NULLIF(rw.returned_orders_total, 0) AS same_day_return_fraction FROM returned_orders_by_week AS rw INNER JOIN positive_margin_weeks AS pmw ON rw.week_start = pmw.week_start ORDER BY rw.week_start

nodes.label: Basket Growth Meets Return Risk
nodes.summary:
Superstore’s clearest growth lever is larger baskets: in the March 2015 surge, average order value rose from $321.95 to $2,217.86 while units per order increased from 7.46 to 12.41, showing customers bought more items and higher-value items at the same time [1]. This is strategically important because the broader business has sustained expansion—annual sales rose from $484.2k in 2015 to $733.2k in 2018 while activity grew from 2.0k to 3.3k orders—so preserving basket quality matters as much as adding volume.

Profitability appears to be improving, with gross margin increasing in 14 of 20 visible weeks, but discount changes moved in the same direction in only about 47% of comparable weeks [7]. The concurrent increase in order value and units supports the view that mix and basket expansion, rather than discounting alone, are contributing to the improvement [6]. Finance should therefore prioritize identifying the products, customer groups, and selling motions behind high-value multi-unit orders before treating broader discount changes as the primary margin lever.

Returns are the immediate operational risk to that growth. Standard Class accounts for the largest revenue concentration, at 59.74, yet First Class has the greatest return concentration, at 10.94 [2]; over the last 12 months, First Class also posted the highest return rate at 7.29%, ahead of Second Class at 6.79%, Standard Class at 5.82%, and Same Day at 5.56% [3]. However, another time comparison puts Same Day highest at roughly 7.2%, demonstrating that the leading problem mode changes by period rather than pointing to a stable single culprit [5][8]. Management should immediately review return reasons and delivery promises by ship mode and time period, with each region’s sole regional manager accountable for execution in Central, East, South, and West [4].
